content: Infantile cortical hyperostosis, also referred to as Caffey disease, is a self-limiting inflammatory condition that affects infants. It is characterized by changes in the bones, swelling of soft tissues, and irritability. The condition may be present at birth or develop shortly thereafter. The exact cause remains unknown, and both familial and sporadic forms of the disease have been identified. Infants with this condition typically exhibit a triad of symptoms: soft-tissue swelling, bone lesions, and irritability. The swelling appears suddenly, is firm and deep, and may be tender to the touch. The bone lesions are often asymmetrical and can involve multiple areas of the body. Commonly affected bones include the mandible (lower jaw), tibia, ulna, clavicle, scapula, ribs, humerus, femur, fibula, skull, ilium, and metatarsals. When the mandible is involved, infants may refuse to eat, which can result in failure to thrive. Diagnosis is primarily based on physical examination, with X-rays used to confirm bone changes and soft tissue swelling. Biopsy of affected areas can reveal characteristic histopathological changes. Although there are no specific blood tests for this condition, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and alkaline phosphatase levels are often observed. A complete blood count may show anemia (low red blood cell count) and leukocytosis (high white blood cell count). Additional tests may be performed to rule out other conditions. In prenatal cases, ultrasound imaging can assist in diagnosis. The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, which is more common and requires urgent treatment. Other conditions that may mimic infantile cortical hyperostosis and need to be excluded include physical trauma, child abuse, Vitamin A toxicity, hyperphosphatemia, prostaglandin E1 and E2 administration, scurvy, infections (such as syphilis), Ewing sarcoma, and metastatic neuroblastoma. In the early stages of the disease, biopsy findings reveal inflammation of the periosteum and adjacent soft tissues. As the inflammation resolves, the periosteum remains thickened, and subperiosteal immature lamellar bone becomes evident. The bone marrow spaces may contain vascular fibrous tissue. Over time, the inflammation and subperiosteal changes subside, and hyperplasia of lamellar cortical bone is observed. Radiographs initially show layers of new periosteal bone formation with cortical thickening. The periosteal new bone may cover the diaphysis of the bone, increasing its diameter. Eventually, the density of the periosteal new bone becomes uniform with the underlying cortex, and the bone remodels to regain a normal appearance. The prognosis for infantile cortical hyperostosis is favorable, as the condition resolves spontaneously without treatment, typically within 6 to 9 months. Long-term complications, such as bone deformities, bony fusions, or limb-length discrepancies, are rare. Epidemiologically, the disease affects approximately 3 in 1000 infants under 6 months of age in the United States. There is no known predilection based on race or sex. Almost all cases occur by the age of 5 months. The familial form of the disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner with variable penetrance. This form tends to have an earlier onset, being present at birth in 24% of cases, with an average onset age of 6 to 8 weeks. The sporadic form typically has an onset age of 9 to 11 weeks. The condition was first described in 1945 by John Caffey, who identified a group of infants presenting with tender soft tissue swelling and cortical thickening of the skeleton, with symptoms appearing within the first three months of life.
